q: Which action is an example of fiscal policy?
r: Congress raising or lowering taxes and government spending
Fiscal policy uses the federal budget.
w: The Federal Reserve changing the interest rate on loans
A company deciding to cut prices on its products
A bank approving a mortgage for a customer

q: Which action is an example of monetary policy?
r: The Federal Reserve adjusting interest rates and the money supply
Monetary policy influences borrowing and spending.
w: Congress passing a new tax law for businesses
The president signing a spending bill
A city council approving a local budget

q: Who conducts monetary policy in the United States?
r: The Federal Reserve
The Fed is the nation's central bank.
w: It supports trade and business data.

q: How does the Fed typically respond to slow economic growth?
r: It lowers interest rates to encourage borrowing and spending
Cheaper credit stimulates activity.
w: It raises interest rates to discourage borrowing
That is used to cool inflation.
It bans all bank lending for a year
It raises taxes on every business
The Fed does not set taxes.

q: How does the Fed typically respond to rapidly rising inflation?
r: It raises interest rates to slow borrowing and spending
Higher rates cool demand.
w: It lowers interest rates to speed up spending
It prints more money for all citizens
The Fed does not set taxes.

q: What is expansionary fiscal policy?
r: Increasing government spending or cutting taxes to boost the economy
It aims to raise demand.
w: Raising taxes and cutting spending to cool the economy
Raising interest rates to slow lending

q: What is contractionary fiscal policy?
r: Raising taxes or cutting spending to slow the economy
It aims to reduce demand and inflation.
w: Lowering interest rates to encourage borrowing

q: What is a budget deficit?
r: When government spending exceeds the revenue it collects in a year
The gap is financed by borrowing.
w: When government revenue exceeds spending in a year
When prices fall across the economy

q: What is the national debt?
r: The total amount the government owes from past borrowing
It is the accumulation of deficits.
w: The amount the government spends in one year
The amount citizens owe on credit cards
The amount of tax collected in a year

q: What is regulation?
r: Rules set by government to control how businesses operate
Examples include safety and environmental standards.
w: Money given by government to help businesses grow
A business owner's personal code of conduct

q: Which agency enforces consumer protection and competition laws in advertising and marketing?
r: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
It guards against unfair or deceptive practices.

q: Which agency sets and enforces workplace safety standards?
r: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
It inspects workplaces and issues fines.

q: Which agency regulates the safety of food, drugs and cosmetics?
r: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
It approves drugs and inspects food.

q: Which agency sets and enforces pollution standards?
r: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
It writes rules for air and water quality.

q: What does the Small Business Administration (SBA) do?
r: Helps small businesses with loan guarantees, counseling and contracts
It supports entrepreneurs.

q: What is antitrust law designed to do?
r: Promote competition and prevent unfair monopolies
It limits price fixing and anticompetitive mergers.

q: Two rival gas stations secretly agree to charge the same high price. Which law is most likely violated?
r: Antitrust law against price fixing
Competitors may not coordinate prices.

q: What is a monopoly?
r: A market in which one seller controls the supply of a product
Few or no substitutes are available.
w: A market with many equal sellers
A market with a few large sellers

q: What is an oligopoly?
r: A market dominated by a few large sellers
Airlines and wireless carriers are examples.
w: A market with thousands of small sellers
That is closer to perfect competition.
That is not a market structure.

q: What is perfect competition?
r: A market with many sellers of identical products and easy entry
No single seller sets the price.
w: A market with one dominant seller
A market with a few large sellers
A market with government price controls only

q: What is monopolistic competition?
r: Many sellers offering similar but differentiated products
Restaurants and clothing shops are examples.
w: One seller with a unique product

q: What is a price ceiling?
r: A legal maximum price that can be charged for a good
Rent control is an example.
w: A legal minimum price that must be charged
The highest price a seller wants
That is not a legal limit.
A tax added to a price

q: If a price ceiling is set below the equilibrium price, what is the likely result?
r: A shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
The low price attracts buyers but discourages sellers.
w: A surplus, because sellers produce too much
That occurs with a price floor above equilibrium.
No effect, because markets ignore laws
A binding ceiling changes the market.
A rise in the equilibrium price

q: What is a price floor?
r: A legal minimum price below which a good cannot be sold
The minimum wage works like a price floor.
w: The lowest price a buyer would like
That is not a legal limit.
A discount offered by a store

q: If a price floor is set above the equilibrium price, what is the likely result?
r: A surplus, because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
The high price attracts sellers but discourages buyers.
w: A shortage, because buyers want more than sellers offer
That occurs with a ceiling below equilibrium.
No effect, because prices adjust instantly
A binding floor changes the market.
A fall in the equilibrium price

q: What is a subsidy?
r: Financial help from the government to producers or consumers
It lowers costs or prices.
w: A fine for breaking a rule

q: Which is an example of a government subsidy?
r: Payments to farmers to support crop production
Producers receive government money.
w: That is a tax on imports.
A fine for polluting a river
A license fee for opening a restaurant

q: What is a tax incentive?
r: A tax reduction offered to encourage a certain behavior
Examples include credits for solar panels.
w: A tax increase to punish a behavior
A fee for using a government service
A rule that bans a product

q: What is a licensing requirement?
r: Government permission needed to operate certain businesses or professions
Doctors and electricians need licenses.
w: A tax paid on business profits
A rule about how to advertise

q: What is the effect of higher business taxes on a firm's decisions?
r: It can reduce investment and hiring because after-tax profit is lower
Firms weigh taxes in their plans.
w: Higher taxes do not guarantee hiring.
It has no effect on any decisions

q: What is a tariff's effect on consumers?
r: Prices of imported goods usually rise
Tariffs add to the cost of foreign products.
w: Prices of imported goods usually fall

q: Which group generally benefits most from a tariff on imported steel?
r: Domestic steel producers, who face less foreign competition
They can sell more or charge more.
w: Consumers who buy products made of steel
Companies that use steel to make goods

q: What is the minimum wage?
r: The lowest hourly pay that employers may legally offer
It is set by law.
w: The average pay across all jobs
The highest pay a worker can earn
That is not a legal maximum.
The pay for part-time workers only

q: Why do economists often debate the minimum wage?
r: It can raise incomes for some workers but may reduce hiring for others
The effects depend on levels and conditions.
w: It has no effect on anyone
It is set by private firms only
It always causes inflation to fall

q: What is the purpose of Social Security?
r: To provide retirement, disability and survivor income
It is funded by payroll taxes.
w: To provide loans to small firms

q: What is a transfer payment?
r: Money given by government to individuals without goods or services in return
Social Security and unemployment benefits are examples.
w: Money paid to a worker for a job
Money paid to a contractor for a road

q: What is an economic indicator?
r: A statistic that shows how well the economy is performing
GDP and unemployment are examples.
w: A tax that is charged on economic activity
A rule that sets prices in markets

q: What does the unemployment rate measure?
r: The percent of the labor force that is jobless and looking for work
It is a key labor market indicator.
w: The percent of all people who have no job
It counts only the labor force.
The number of new jobs created last year
The average wage paid to workers

q: If the labor force is 200 million and 10 million are unemployed, what is the unemployment rate?
r: 10 divided by 200 equals 0.05.
w: This is the number of unemployed in millions.

q: Who is counted as part of the labor force?
r: People who are employed or actively looking for work
Both groups are in the labor force.
w: Only people who have a full-time job
Part-time and unemployed job seekers also count.
All people over the age of 16
Some are not working or looking.

q: What does the Consumer Price Index (CPI) measure?
r: Changes in the average price of a basket of consumer goods and services
It is the main gauge of inflation.
w: The total value of goods produced in a country
The number of people with jobs

q: The CPI rises from 200 to 210 over a year. What is the inflation rate?
r: The increase of 10 divided by 200 is 5%.
w: This treats the point change as a percent.
This is not the result of the formula.
This is not the result of the formula.

q: What does the Producer Price Index (PPI) measure?
r: Changes in the prices that producers receive for their goods
It can signal future consumer inflation.
w: Changes in the prices consumers pay

q: What does GDP growth rate show?
r: How fast the economy's output is expanding or shrinking
Positive growth means expansion.

q: What is a recession commonly defined as in the news?
r: Two consecutive quarters of declining GDP
It is a common rule of thumb.
w: One day of falling stock prices

q: What is a depression?
r: A very severe and prolonged downturn in economic activity
The Great Depression of the 1930s is an example.
w: A period of fast economic growth
A drop in the price of one product

q: What is the consumer confidence index?
r: A measure of how optimistic consumers are about the economy
Confident consumers tend to spend more.
w: A measure of how many goods stores sell
A measure of bank interest rates

q: What do housing starts measure?
r: The number of new residential construction projects begun
They signal demand and confidence.
w: The number of homes sold last year
The average price of a home
The number of renters in a city

q: Which is a leading indicator of the economy?
r: New building permits
They tend to change before the overall economy does.
w: Consumer price inflation after the fact
Past GDP is a lagging measure.

q: Which is a lagging indicator of the economy?
r: The unemployment rate
It usually changes after the economy turns.
w: They tend to lead the economy.

q: What is the federal funds rate?
r: The interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans
The Fed targets it to guide the economy.
w: The interest rate on a home mortgage
The tax rate on federal income

q: What does the stock market index, such as the S&P 500, measure?
r: The combined performance of a group of large company stocks
It reflects investor sentiment.
w: The price of one company's stock
That is a single stock price.
The total debt of the government
The number of jobs in the economy

q: What is the trade balance?
r: The difference between a country's exports and imports
A deficit means imports exceed exports.
w: The total amount of tariffs collected
The number of trade agreements signed
That is not the trade balance.

q: Why can a low unemployment rate sometimes lead to higher inflation?
r: Tight labor markets can push wages and prices up
Employers compete for scarce workers.

q: What is stagflation?
r: High inflation combined with high unemployment and slow growth
It is difficult for policymakers to fix.

q: What does disposable income mean?
r: Income left after paying taxes, available to spend or save
It drives consumer spending.
w: Income before any taxes are paid

q: What does per capita GDP measure?
r: Economic output divided by the number of people
It shows average output per person.
w: Total output of the largest firms
That is not per capita GDP.

q: What is globalization?
r: The growing connection of the world's economies through trade and investment
Goods, money and ideas cross borders.
w: The growth of a single country's local market
The ban on trading with other countries
The merger of all countries into one

q: Why do countries trade with one another?
r: To obtain goods and services they cannot produce as cheaply or at all
Trade can raise living standards.
w: To prevent other countries from growing
Trade is not meant to prevent growth.

q: What is the main benefit of specialization and trade?
r: Greater total output and lower prices for consumers
Countries focus on what they do best.
w: Higher import taxes for all countries

q: Country A can make cloth at a lower opportunity cost than Country B, while Country B can grow wheat at a lower opportunity cost. What should they do?
r: A should specialize in cloth, B in wheat, and they should trade
Each exports where it has comparative advantage.
w: Each country should make both goods alone
A should make wheat and B should make cloth
Neither should trade with the other

q: What is an exchange rate?
r: The price of one currency in terms of another
It changes with supply and demand.
w: The interest rate on foreign loans

q: If the U.S. dollar strengthens against the euro, imports from Europe become:
r: Cheaper for Americans
Each dollar buys more euros.
w: This is the effect of a weaker dollar.

q: What is outsourcing?
r: Hiring another company, often abroad, to perform work
It can lower costs.
w: Producing all goods inside the company
Selling shares of stock to the public
Building a new factory at home

q: What is offshoring?
r: Moving business operations to another country
Companies seek lower costs or new markets.
w: Moving operations to another city at home
Merging with a rival at home

q: What is a trade bloc?
r: A group of countries that agree to reduce trade barriers among themselves
The EU is an example.
w: A group of companies that fix prices
A group of banks that lend to governments
A group of workers that bargains for pay

q: What is the primary goal of the World Trade Organization (WTO)?
r: To help trade flow smoothly and settle trade disputes
It sets rules among member nations.
w: To set the price of oil worldwide
To lend money to poor countries
To collect taxes from all nations

q: What is a cartel?
r: A group of producers that agree to control prices or output
OPEC is a well-known example.
w: A group of consumers that boycott a product
A group of workers in a union
A government agency that regulates trade

q: What is balance of payments?
r: A record of all money flowing into and out of a country
It includes trade, investment and transfers.
w: A record of a company's yearly profit
A list of taxes paid by citizens
A statement of government debt only

q: Which is an example of foreign direct investment?
r: A car company building a factory in another country
It is a long-term investment in operations abroad.
w: A tourist buying a souvenir abroad
A company paying a customs duty
A bank lending money for one year
That is lending, not direct investment.

q: What is a trade barrier?
r: Any government measure that makes trade across borders more difficult
Tariffs and quotas are examples.
w: A river that crosses a border

q: Which is a non-tariff barrier to trade?
r: A strict product standard that foreign goods struggle to meet
Rules can limit trade without a tax.

q: What is protectionism?
r: Government policies that shield domestic industries from foreign competition
Tariffs and quotas are tools.
w: Government policies that remove all trade barriers
Government rules that protect consumers from fraud

q: What is a common argument for protectionism?
r: It protects domestic jobs in industries facing foreign competition
Supporters stress job security.
w: It lowers prices for all consumers

q: What is a common argument against protectionism?
r: It raises prices for consumers and can invite retaliation
Other countries may respond with their own tariffs.
w: It lowers the cost of imports

q: What is a free trade agreement?
r: A treaty in which countries reduce or remove tariffs and other trade barriers
The USMCA is an example.
w: A treaty in which countries raise tariffs on each other
A treaty in which countries agree to stop all trade
A treaty in which countries share their armies

q: What is a currency devaluation?
r: A decrease in the official value of a currency
It can make exports cheaper.
w: An increase in the official value of a currency
A new design of the banknotes
A ban on using the currency
